claims.text: High configurational entropy maintains the chemical and structural stability of multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions.
High configurational entropy suppresses phase segregation and ordering in these nanoparticles.
Atomic-size mismatch in near-equiatomic nanoparticles produces local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions generate elastic strain fields.
Elastic strain fields arising from local lattice distortions mediate high-temperature stabilization.
Configurational entropy and local elastic strain fields kinetically inhibit atomic diffusion.
Slower atomic diffusion inhibits phase segregation and preserves a homogeneous solid-solution structure.
Atomic diffusion typically triggers phase separation at elevated temperatures.
A post-synthesis annealing treatment will enhance atomic mobility and initiate segregation.
Diffusion-driven phase transformations are expected under catalytic temperatures of 773–1173 K and thermoelectric temperatures of 473–1923 K.
Nanoparticles that retain a homogeneous high-entropy state will exhibit minimal phase segregation.
Preservation of the homogeneous solid-solution structure maintains stable and predictable catalytic or thermoelectric properties.
Annealed nanoparticles will show more phase separation, altered elemental distributions, and degraded catalytic or thermoelectric performance than as-synthesized controls.
The proposed stabilization requires sufficiently small nanoparticles.
Increasing nanoparticle size reduces the impact of strain fields.
At sufficiently extreme temperatures, diffusion can overcome the proposed stabilizing barriers.
